hero.name: Randy Weston
hero.lede: A Brooklyn pianist who followed the music back to Africa: to Tangier, where he ran the African Rhythms club, to the Gnawa musicians of Morocco, to Egypt, Japan and the Mississippi Delta. This page gathers what he said in his 2009 Smithsonian oral history, and what the musicians who knew him said in theirs.

quote.q: So, all of my compositions, all of my music is based upon love, history, and family, and respect.
marks: So, all of my compositions, all of my music is based upon love, history, and family, and respect.

categories.label: What Music Is
categories.definition: His ideas about music itself: what it is, where it came from at the creation, what it does to people and to the planet, and what his own music is built on. The idea is the point, not the occasion or the record.

categories.label: Africa the Source
categories.definition: Africa as the origin and spiritual centre of the music and of humanity: the continent, its ancient civilisations, its traditional music, and the music African peoples created wherever they were taken.

categories.label: Ancestors and Destiny
categories.definition: The forebears who survived the crossing and slavery, what he owes them, and his sense that their spirits and the creator have guided his life, including the honours that came to him late.

categories.label: Family and Brooklyn
categories.definition: His parents, his sister and the Brooklyn household he grew up in: what they taught him, how they lived, and his sister's death and funeral.

categories.label: The Masters
categories.definition: The great musicians of the generations before him as he knew them: his idols, the ones he met and touched, what they did and endured, and the baton they passed to him.

categories.label: At the Piano
categories.definition: His own instrument and how he plays it: solo, trio and orchestra, how he came to play solo, his reluctance about it, and pianos he has loved.

categories.label: Records and Compositions
categories.definition: The albums of these years and the pieces on them: what the titles mean, why each was made, where and why he composed, and how the music was arranged and recorded, including his partnership with his arranger.

categories.label: Morocco and the Gnawa
categories.definition: Morocco, its peoples, and the Gnawa musicians: who they are, their instruments and spiritual practice, what playing with them taught him, and his Moroccan ventures from the Tangier festival to the trip up the mountain.

categories.label: On the Road
categories.definition: Concerts and travels outside Morocco and apart from his marriage: festivals and residencies, Japan and its shrine, an English cathedral, a library opening in Egypt, and how he moves among people when he travels.

categories.label: His Marriage
categories.definition: How he met and married his wife: her shop in Paris, the trip to Egypt they took together, the sudden proposal, the Nubian wedding and its aftermath.

items.what: For a French–Spanish television documentary about his life in Morocco, he brought his sextet over and spent time with three traditional groups: the Gnawa, a Sufi brotherhood living in Tangier, and the musicians of Jajouka in the Rif Mountains.

items.title: By donkey up the mountain to Jajouka
items.q: Seeing these guys going up the mountains on these donkeys, with their instruments, that was incredible. Benny said, “We have adventure! We have adventure!”
marks: Seeing these guys going up the mountains on these donkeys, with their instruments, that was incredible. Benny said, “We have adventure! We have adventure!”
items.what: During the film shoot the band had to ride donkeys up the mountain to the village of Jajouka, where the musicians are great healers who play the lira, a flute. Only Billy Harper, from Texas, knew how to ride, and Benny Powell cried 'We have adventure!'. The village had no electricity and no lights, they saw rites of passage, and the band stayed and had a great time.

items.title: The 1972 festival in the Tangier bullring
items.q: We had this three-day festival at a bullring in Tangiers. Two nights it was at the bullring and the next night it was a Sahara sandstorm coming from the Sahara. We couldn’t play in the bull right so we had to rush and clean up this theatre called Theatre Cervantes in Tangiers.

At the temple, with its walls carved with ancient musical instruments, an antiquities inspector, Shadley, befriended them. He took them to the Nubian Museum and introduced them to its head.

items.title: A Nubian wedding near Aswan
items.q: We got there and the next thing we hear is drums. All of the sudden, the whole village, they put us on thrones. These thrones are made out of cardboard, all the musicians came and they partied all night. We did a Nubian ceremony, a Nubian marriage. It was something, some kind of adventure.

items.what: On a return trip to Egypt right after his NEA Jazz Masters award, sitting in a hotel with Fatou and Shadley, he was moved by the spirit to say 'I want to marry this woman'. Shadley took them to a Nubian village, dressed them in Nubian clothes and had them photographed as a Nubian couple. The whole village came with drums, seated them on cardboard thrones and partied all night in a Nubian marriage ceremony. Afterwards he had to telephone Fatou's Muslim father, whose own father had been an imam.

items.title: Ten days in the Mississippi Delta
items.q: Now I’ve written 40 blues, I thought I knew the blues, but I didn’t know the blues until I went to Mississippi. I saw the slave shacks; I physically saw a cotton field.

items.what: He and his wife spent ten days in the Mississippi Delta. He had written 40 blues but said he did not know the blues until he saw the slave shacks and a cotton field almost two football fields wide, and thought of ancestors forced to meet a rising quota. It left him amazed and grateful at what they went through 'to produce a Randy Weston'.

He met the pipa player Min Xiao-Fen through her work with a Senegalese musician in Atlanta. Dr. Wayne Chandler's book Ancient Future and a Guggenheim exhibition of Shang masks convinced them both of an ancient Africa–China connection, and the record was built to make that connection. items.q: One of the first live bands I saw was at a left-wing union dance where Randy Weston had the band and Ahmed was the bass player.
marks: One of the first live bands I saw was at a left-wing union dance where Randy Weston had the band and Ahmed was the bass player.

items.name: Hubert Laws
items.line: first went to africa because of him
items.q: First time I went to Africa was because of Randy Weston.
marks: First time I went to Africa was because of Randy Weston.

items.name: Orrin Keepnews
items.line: had him in the studio before monk
items.q: before I got involved with Thelonious I had been in the studio with people like Randy Weston, Mundell Lowe, Billy Taylor, you know all pussycats.
items.note: ‘Pussycats’ means easy to work with; he has just called Monk ‘a real tough cookie’.
marks: before I got involved with Thelonious I had been in the studio with people like Randy Weston, Mundell Lowe, Billy Taylor, you know all pussycats.
items.src: Hamilton College, Fillius Jazz Archive, interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2002

items.name: Orrin Keepnews
items.line: had his albums on the office wall
items.q: he said, “Oh, Randy! I’m glad somebody got around to recording him. It should have been done along time ago,”
items.note: The words are Miles Davis’s, as Keepnews recalls them.
marks: he said, “Oh, Randy! I’m glad somebody got around to recording him. It should have been done along time ago,”

items.name: Jimmy Owens
items.line: learned the publishing business from him
items.q: Randy Weston was one of my mentors also. He taught me a lot about the business — publishing, and how publishing works.
marks: Randy Weston was one of my mentors also. He taught me a lot about the business — publishing, and how publishing works.
items.src: Hamilton College, Fillius Jazz Archive, interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2001

items.name: Annie Ross
items.line: loved his pieces on “high flyin’”
items.q: I loved “High Flyin’” which didn’t get that much distribution but it was a good album, and those things of Randy Weston’s are wonderful.
items.note: ‘High Flyin’’ is the Lambert, Hendricks & Ross album on which she sang his tunes.
marks: I loved “High Flyin’” which didn’t get that much distribution but it was a good album, and those things of Randy Weston’s are wonderful.
items.src: Hamilton College, Fillius Jazz Archive, interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2001

items.name: Jack DeJohnette
items.q: they used to bring flatbed trucks up into Harlem and they'd have concerts up there. I used to go hear Randy Weston play there.
marks: they used to bring flatbed trucks up into Harlem and they'd have concerts up there. I used to go hear Randy Weston play there.

items.name: Jackie McLean
items.line: named him among the brooklyn players at sessions
items.q: So there were guys from Brooklyn that would come over and play. Randy Weston. We used to go to Brooklyn, to jam sessions over there.
marks: So there were guys from Brooklyn that would come over and play. Randy Weston. We used to go to Brooklyn, to jam sessions over there.

items.name: Wendy Oxenhorn
items.line: called him one of the spiritual leaders
items.q: Him, and Randy Weston and Jimmy Heath, these spiritual... They’re spiritual leaders, is what they are.
items.note: ‘Him’ is Sonny Rollins; the praise is for three men.
marks: Him, and Randy Weston and Jimmy Heath, these spiritual... They’re spiritual leaders, is what they are.
